For a year Nazia had blamed 'those tech-park people' for everything in Bengaluru: the rents, the traffic, her landlord's new rules. Online she called them locusts.
Then, on a wet Tuesday evening, her scooter died on the Outer Ring Road. Cars sprayed past. A young woman in a company lanyard pulled over, held an umbrella over the engine while Nazia tried the kick-start, then called a mechanic she knew and waited forty minutes with her.
Her name was Bidisha. She'd moved from Siliguri two years ago. She shared a flat with three others because the rent was too high for her, too.
'Rent's too high for you as well?' Nazia said, surprised.
'Everyone I know is struggling,' Bidisha said. 'Where are you from?'
On the way home, Nazia didn't open the forums. She found herself wondering about Bidisha's flat, her three flatmates, her family in Siliguri. She had a question she wanted to ask her.

qa.q: How long did Bidisha wait with Nazia?
qa.a: She waited forty minutes with her.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling on the way home?
qa.a: She felt curious and a little unsettled, wondering about Bidisha's life instead of opening the forums.

qa.q: Why did this encounter shift Nazia more than an argument might have?
qa.a: A kind act and a calm conversation showed that 'those tech-park people' were real people with the same problems, sparking curiosity instead of defensiveness.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see Nazia, knowing nothing of her online posts?
qa.a: Bidisha simply sees a stranded person who needed help and was friendly, perhaps someone she could chat with again.

grounding: It shows a kind act and a calm conversation with someone from a hated group showing the category has people in it, sparking curiosity.

'Jeevan-da, you seen this? Those colony people again. Every one of them.'
'Show me.' Jeevan put down his tea and actually watched the video. 'Hm. Who made it?'
'Does it matter? It's true.'
'Maybe. I'm just curious.' Jeevan scratched his beard. 'You've been angry at them for a year, Anirban. Have you met one?'
'Why would I?'
'I'm asking honestly. Name one.'
A pause. 'There's a guy at the gym. Sanjay. He's from there.'
'What's he like?'
Another pause. 'He spots me on the bench press. Helped me with my back last month.'
'So Sanjay's okay.'
'Sanjay's different.'
'Maybe. How many of them have you met who weren't different?'
Anirban opened his mouth, then closed it.
'I'm not trying to win,' Jeevan said. 'I just want to know what you think. Not what the video thinks.'
Anirban looked at the paused screen for a while. 'I'll ask Sanjay where he grew up.'

qa.q: Who spots Anirban on the bench press?
qa.a: Sanjay, a guy at the gym, spots him.

qa.q: What is Anirban feeling when he opens his mouth, then closes it?
qa.a: He seems caught off guard and unsure, as his idea of 'every one of them' meets the real person he knows.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan's curious questioning work better than trying to win the argument?
qa.a: Jeevan stays calm and asks about real people, so Anirban isn't defensive and starts thinking for himself.

qa.q: What might Sanjay experience if Anirban asks him where he grew up?
qa.a: Sanjay may be surprised but pleased to be seen as a person, and the conversation could build a real friendship.

grounding: It shows a family member who still listens and asks curious questions, helping someone see that a hated category is made of real people.
